reason: Bankjoy's live VP of Engineering posting confesses the exact inflection Daniel fixes — eight engineering value streams with no CTO in seat, a QA org of eight manual plus two automation engineers, and an explicit ask for someone who has 'personally rescued or rebuilt automation programs' and can drive 'manual-heavy to automation-first' in a regulated fintech.

company.name: Bankjoy
company.one_liner: Digital banking platform (mobile/online banking, account opening, loan origination, conversational AI, fraud) sold to community banks and credit unions; 85+ client institutions, 150+ integrations.
company.industry: Fintech / digital banking software (B2B SaaS to community FIs)
company.stage: Growth-stage venture-backed — YC W15, Bessemer Venture Partners, Curql Collective; ~$14.4M raised across 6 rounds (aggregator); ~60-70 employees
company.hq: Royal Oak, Michigan (Detroit metro), USA — remote roles posted in US and Canada

evidence_jobs.title: VP of Engineering
evidence_jobs.quote: The ideal candidate has deep roots in quality engineering, has personally rescued or rebuilt automation programs in multi-platform environments, and has the organizational credibility to drive a shift from manual-heavy to automation-first quality culture.

people_spec: Founder & CEO (Michael Duncan) — owns the hire and the growth-inflection framing
Founder & COO (Weiwei Duncan) — the posting names the COO as the peer this role sits alongside in senior leadership
VP of Engineering, Platform (Brent VanderMeide) — the posting names the VP of Platform Engineering as the cross-cutting partner on AI coding adoption, release coordination and DevOps
Sr. Director of Engineering (Yanli Zhao) — runs delivery inside the value streams today
Note: there is no sitting CTO — the last named CTO (Michael Carroll, appointed Sep 2022) is listed as former, so do not look for one
talk_track: I ran platform and reliability engineering at Tricentis, a software-testing company, after leading QA automation and developer platforms at PayPal and Ripple — my whole career has been moving release quality out of people's hands and into systems. Your VP of Engineering posting asks for someone who has "personally rescued or rebuilt automation programs in multi-platform environments" and can shift the org from "manual-heavy to automation-first," and it says the role leads a QA organization of eight manual QA engineers and two automation QA engineers across eight value streams. The number to read there is the ratio, not the title: with quality capacity that manual, each new value stream adds QA headcount instead of amortizing it, so cost-to-deliver climbs in step with the client count you keep announcing. The instinct is to hire more automation engineers; the cheaper first move is release gates plus a test-data and environment-parity layer, so the ten people you already have produce automation as a byproduct of the work they do anyway. That reorders the hiring plan rather than enlarging it, which is worth knowing whether or not you ever talk to me. Is the ratio something you have already priced in? — Daniel Kirichanski, Prime Path Global
